newsitem.title: USA: Avis denies charges of bias against Jews.
newsitem.headline: Avis denies charges of bias against Jews.

text.p: Avis Rent-A-Car Wednesday denied it told employees to discriminate against Jews, saying the allegations were part of a campaign by lawyers trying to intimidate the company into settling a racial discrimination case.
"The allegation that Avis instructed employees to discriminate against Jews is ridiculous and completely false," the company, a unit of HFS Inc., said in a statement.

Avis said the lawyers apparently wanted to force a settlement of a racial bias lawsuit filed by three black women last year against Avis and a franchisee. The case, filed in Raleigh, N.C., is pending.
The car rental company claimed the lawyers were using the media to "sully Avis' reputation ... to intimidate Avis, to extract an unjustifiably large settlement and to deprive it of a fair trial."

Avis was responding to a USA Today report that supervisors told workers at Avis' customer service center in Tulsa, Okla., as recently as last month to avoid giving corporate accounts or discounts to certain Jewish-owned businesses.

Six former Avis workers from the corporate accounts department said they were told to "watch out for yeshivas," a Hebrew word meaning school, the paper said. Workers said it became the code word for businesses owned by orthodox Jews.
Agents who worked in the 15-employee department say they were told to listen for accents and be suspicious of callers from heavily Jewish areas, such as New York, USA Today said.
In a sworn statement filed this week in connection with the racial bias suit, former Avis employee Elaine Rodgers said, "Telesales agents used the word "yeshiva" to refer to Hassidic Jews."

Avis said the charges apparently related to past instances where cars were rented under corporate accounts but were used by underage drivers for improper purposes and returned with a higher than normal rate of collision-related damage.
"Specifically, callers frequently claimed to be employed by yeshivas when they, in fact, were not," the statement said.

"They then showed up with fistfulls of coupons and got cars from us," added Avis Executive Vice President John Carley in an interview. "We found that they were not affilated with the yeshivas and were using the cars against our rules, for taxis, hauling garbage and, in one case, as a hearse."
To curb such incidents, Avis said it alerted the department.

"Once questions arose about the way in which the problem was being solved, Avis immediately clarified its underage renter policy in order to avoid even the appearance of discrimination," the company said.
Carley said the lawyers were "hoping we will cave and settle" but Avis will fight the allegations in court.
"I want to try this case next week," he said.
HFS stock fell $1.125 to $66.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
